conversations.title: Pain, Gender, and Cultural Endurance Norms

turns.text:
I've been having a conversation with GPT 5.6 and this a summary. I want to get other models opinions and sort of explore this more here. "We started with “women probably have higher pain tolerance, therefore maybe women helped create ‘man up,’” and somehow ended up with a miniature anthropology of suffering. Typical Tuesday.

Here’s the clean version.

The first thing we had to separate was that “pain tolerance” is not one thing. We had been bundling together pain threshold, pain tolerance, pain sensitivity, ability to function while hurting, willingness to display pain, chronic pain burden, and culturally learned expectations about what you’re supposed to do when you hurt. Those can move independently, and sometimes in opposite directions.

On the biological/experimental side, the simple popular claim that women naturally have higher pain tolerance than men does not hold up well. Controlled pain studies generally find men showing higher average thresholds and tolerance for several kinds of experimentally induced pain. That does not mean men are universally “tougher,” nor does it settle how much of the difference is biological versus learned gender behavior.

Meanwhile, women tend to carry a greater burden of many kinds of pain, including higher rates of a number of chronic pain conditions plus menstruation, pregnancy, childbirth, and so on. So there is an important distinction:

Experiencing more pain over a lifetime ≠ having a nervous system that requires more stimulation before pain becomes intolerable.

Then chronic pain complicated it further. Repeated pain does not simply train someone into physiological invulnerability. Chronic pain can actually make the nervous system more sensitive, through things like central sensitization. Habituation can happen too, but it depends on the condition and stimulus.

So a person who has lived with back pain for forty years may actually have a more sensitive pain system while simultaneously being vastly better at functioning while in pain.

That distinction turns out to be crucial.

A person can learn:

> “This hurts badly, but I recognize it, I know I'm not dying, I know what I can still do, and dinner isn't going to make itself.”



That is not necessarily higher biological pain tolerance. It's experience, emotional regulation, interpretation, practiced coping, suppression of outward behavior, duty, and functional persistence.

And those things absolutely can be socially learned.

Children observe how adults respond to pain. Parents can model “shake it off,” catastrophize minor injuries, minimize suffering, provide lots of attention for pain, or demonstrate calm persistence. Kids learn not just what pain feels like but what pain means and what you're supposed to do about it.

That gives us a plausible intergenerational mechanism that isn't inherently gendered:

pain happens → competent adults keep functioning → children watch → children inherit the rule → they eventually teach it to their children.

Then cultures attach gender-specific meanings to that underlying endurance norm.

Historically, masculinity often has involved some version of proving adulthood through courage, hardship, danger, self-control, or painful initiation. Anthropology gives us plenty of societies where boys have to demonstrate that they can endure something difficult before being recognized as men.

But that does not mean “real men don't feel pain” has been a universal human constant.

Men in various historical periods have openly wept, lamented, expressed suffering, and remained perfectly recognizable as masculine. Even within Western history, ideals of male emotional expression have changed dramatically.

So there appears to be an important historical difference between:

“A man doesn't feel/show pain.”

and the older, broader idea:

“A man proves himself by continuing despite pain.”

Those aren't the same norm.

Women also historically developed their own endurance script, often less about heroic danger and more about patient suffering and continued responsibility. Motherhood, caregiving, chronic ailments, childbirth, domestic labor, economic necessity, etc. can produce something like:

> “Yes, it hurts. That's life. Things still have to get done.”



So rather than one gender possessing an endurance culture and imposing it on the other, you can plausibly have two overlapping traditions of endurance:

male-coded: endure danger/hardship, maintain control, fulfill duty.

female-coded: endure suffering/discomfort, keep caring for people, fulfill duty.

Notice the common denominator: fulfill duty despite pain.

And that gets us back to “man up.”

There is no good reason to model that norm as exclusively:

men → boys/men.

Men certainly enforce masculine norms on one another. Fathers, coaches, soldiers, peers, institutions, etc. matter enormously.

But mothers, girlfriends, wives, sisters, teachers, daughters, and women generally also evaluate male behavior. Masculinity is partly a social status, which means it depends upon other people's judgments. Women aren't somehow outside the culture of masculinity simply because they aren't men.

So a woman who has spent decades functioning through migraines, menstruation, childbirth, caregiving, chronic back pain, whatever, can perfectly coherently think:

> “I have dealt with worse than this and kept going. Why aren't you?”



And if the culture already says male adulthood involves toughness, that can easily become:

> “Come on. Be a man.”



She doesn't need to have biologically higher pain tolerance for that process to occur. Her relevant comparison is her history of functioning while suffering.

Likewise, Grandpa with a wrecked knee can tell his grandson to quit crying because Grandpa worked forty years while hurting.

Grandma can tell her granddaughter the same thing because she raised five children while hurting.

Both are passing down an endurance ethic.

Which gets us to the ideological question we kept bumping into.

Calling something “patriarchal” in academic language does not necessarily mean:

> “Men invented this and imposed it upon women.”



Women can transmit and enforce norms within patriarchal systems. Men can suffer under those systems. Social systems aren't neatly partitioned by the chromosomes of whoever speaks the rule aloud.

But in popular discourse, that distinction often gets lost. “Patriarchy produces masculine stoicism” can mutate into something much simpler:

“Men did this to men.”

Then some hypermasculine or manosphere discourse responds with the mirror image:

“No, women demand this from men.”

Both sides can produce anecdotes proving their preferred direction because both directions actually occur.

That's why neither makes a very satisfying total explanation.

The better causal model is something like:

ecological necessity + dangerous work + caregiving + reproduction + economic pressure + family expectations + gender roles + peer enforcement + mate expectations + institutions + repeated social learning → endurance norms → those norms get transmitted by men and women → different cultures gender them differently → later generations inherit them without knowing why they exist.

Nobody necessarily sat down and invented the rule.

Some parts probably arose because they were genuinely adaptive. A hunter, soldier, farmer, sailor, mother, caregiver, or laborer sometimes does need to continue despite discomfort. There is real value in teaching:

> “Pain doesn't automatically mean stop.”



The problem happens when that useful rule expands into:

> “Pain should never matter.”



or:

> “Displaying suffering means you're morally deficient.”



or:

> “Competent adults shouldn't need help.”



That is where resilience turns into neglect.

So the thing I think survives our increasingly obnoxious encounter with the evidence is basically this:

There is no strong basis for saying women are biologically built to tolerate more pain. There is good reason to think men and women can acquire very strong learned capacities for functioning through pain, especially after years of unavoidable suffering and responsibility. Those coping norms are transmitted intergenerationally. Cultures then attach different gender meanings to endurance. Masculine stoicism has deep historical roots, but its exact form has changed enormously. And both men and women participate in maintaining gender expectations, so reducing “man up” culture to something one sex simply did to the other is almost certainly too crude.

The really useful distinction we uncovered is probably:

Pain sensitivity is biological/psychological.
Pain coping is learned and biological.
Pain expression is social and psychological.
Pain endurance can be practiced.
Pain expectations are cultural.
Gender tells people what all of those are supposed to mean.

Once those get separated, the apparent contradictions mostly stop being contradictions."

Can you see the reports of Google basically open sourcing the fruit fly stuff recently, like last month?
You should look up Alphafold, and recent things related to OpenAI and Navier Stokes.
I just wonder if AI getting better at biology, agentic discovery, and stuff like that might shorten the timespan between the fruit fly and the human brain. You know?
